Heading: Zelenskyy urges US to speed up Patriot deliveries
DNU Summary: Washington approved the sale of 500 interceptors, but Kyiv says delivery may take years.
Body:
Washington approved the sale of 500 interceptors to counter Russian ballistic missile attacks.

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked the U.S. for approving the sale of Patriot interceptors but urged Washington to fast-track the delivery of the defensive missiles.

Zelenskyy praised the “strong decision” by the U.S. to approve the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 interceptors to counter Russian ballistic missiles — but said the years-long wait to deliver them was too long for Ukraine's urgent needs.

“It has been stipulated that deliveries may begin ONLY IN A FEW YEARS,” Zelenskyy wrote in a Facebook post on Friday night.

“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” he added.

Patriot interceptors are crucial for Ukraine to defend itself against Russia’s ballistic missiles, amid fears that Moscow will ramp up its attacks on energy facilities to bring winter blackouts in Ukraine.

In the Facebook post, Zelenskyy said an immediate delivery of Patriot interceptors would allow Ukraine to defend its energy infrastructure during the winter season.

“Providing them to Ukraine right now – in the winter of 2026–2027 – and replenishing our partners’ arsenals LATER, in THE FOLLOWING YEARS” would be the right approach, Zelenskyy said.

The U.S. decision to sell the interceptors signals a thaw in relations between the White House and Kyiv after tensions escalated in recent months.

However, the White House said that it won't pay for the Patriot interceptors. "The estimated total cost is $2.1 billion funded entirely by partners and allies," a statement from the State Department said.

Heading: Oleshky evacuees reunite with families after truce allows crossing back into Ukraine
DNU Summary: The rescue operation began Friday under a local truce, with evacuees travelling through Russia and Belarus.
Body:
Evacuees from Russian-occupied Oleshky have been reunited with their families after crossing into Ukrainian-held territory on Saturday.

The major rescue operation began on Friday and was carried out under the most significant truce since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago.

Evacuees wrapped in Ukrainian flags stepped off buses at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border to be reunited with family members. Volunteers with hand-drawn welcome signs handed coffee to the weary people who had travelled by bus and plane through Russia and Belarus. Residents of nearby villages lined the highway waving flags and torches to greet the convoy.

Tetiana Leonidivna, 71, thanked the Ukrainian soldiers who helped her to flee. “We love them, we love them,” she said through tears. “We know that they are protecting us. And a deep bow to them, and a deep bow to their parents, for having such children. I am proud, I am simply proud.”

The ceasefire in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region began early on Tuesday and was expected to continue through Sunday evening. The White House said the first lady Melania Trump helped broker the localised deal, while Pope Leo XIV pressed Russia and Ukraine to allow aid deliveries and evacuations.

Relatives and volunteers with the Red Cross, Médecins Sans Frontières and World Central Kitchen welcomed the evacuees as they arrived at the border, ready to provide aid and food, including for their pets.

Holding a cigarette between shaking fingers, 48-year-old Ivan Yevhenovych described his last months in Oleshky. “It was very difficult. There were a lot of drones. It was hard to move around the streets,” he said. “Since spring, there hasn’t really been any staple food left. People had a little bit of their own reserves. We are thrifty people.”

He said landmines or drone strikes were killing residents every day.

An estimated 2,000 people remained in Oleshky when the temporary truce took hold. They were offered the choice of being evacuated to Ukrainian- or Russian-held territory, or remaining in the city with replenished food and medical supplies.

“Many people stayed behind and didn’t want to leave,” Yevhenovych said. “Some for their houses, some for their animals.”

Ukrainian authorities, seeking to protect those who remained and safeguard future humanitarian missions, have not said how many residents evacuated Oleshky and have restricted details of their route. Melania Trump posted on social media on Friday that the humanitarian convoy could safely evacuate more than 750 people.

Liza Paliy, 19, waited at the border for her father, whom she last saw more than two and a half years earlier when she fled the occupied city with her mother and sister. “We thought at that time that it would be a month, two maximum, and we would return, but unfortunately two years have already passed,” she said.

Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, hailed the humanitarian mission as a win.

“This is an extremely important moment. Behind us are difficult negotiations, agreements, preparations, and an enormous amount of work. But most importantly, the people who waited so long to be rescued are finally safe,” he said in an online post.

Lubinets said evacuees ranged in age from just over one year old to 94, and they brought pets, including dogs, cats, a parrot and a raccoon. He said he hoped the Oleshky truce could be replicated elsewhere, saying it “could form the basis of a new mechanism for responding to the most difficult humanitarian crises”.

Yana Lantratova, Russia’s human rights commissioner, said both sides have agreed to conduct regular humanitarian missions in and around Oleshky. Lubinets did not mention this development.

“The mission has concluded, but, unfortunately, living conditions in Oleshky remain extremely difficult,” she said. “We will make every effort to support those residents who have made the decision to stay.”

Some Oleshky evacuees who chose to move to Russian-occupied territory were taken to a temporary shelter in Simferopol, Lantratova said. The city is in Ukraine’s Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.

“After everything they have endured and a long journey, it is essential for these people to rest, recover and feel cared for. However, support should not be limited to just a roof over their heads and a hot meal,” she said in a social media post.

A Ukrainian drone attack killed a 30-year-old woman and a 41-year-old man in Russia’s western Bryansk region, the local governor, Yegor Kovalchuk, said on Saturday. Five others were wounded, he said.

Local officials also reported Ukrainian drone attacks in the Russian republic of Bashkortostan. Russian media outlets said there was a fire in the region’s capital, Ufa, home to several oil refineries.

The Russian defence ministry said on Saturday its forces had shot down 433 Ukrainian drones overnight.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said Moscow launched drone attacks on energy and railway infrastructure across Ukraine overnight, leaving 280,000 households in Dnipro and Kyiv regions without power.

Heading: Turkiye’s Erdogan urges Russia and Ukraine to stop Black Sea attacks
DNU Summary: He and Zelenskyy agreed to work on a new grain corridor through the waterway.
Body:
Turkish president hosts Zelenskyy in Istanbul as the two leaders agree to work on a new Black Sea grain corridor.

Turkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has urged both Russia and Ukraine to stop targeting civilian ships in the Black Sea, as he and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy agreed to work on a new grain corridor through the waterway.

Erdogan made the comments on Saturday at a joint news conference with Zelenskyy in Istanbul, saying attacks on civilian vessels were unacceptable, whoever carries them out.

The talks came on the same day US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was growing international interest in a limited ceasefire in the Black Sea to secure grain and energy shipments by both countries.

“It is clear that attacks against civilian vessels and actions that further escalate tensions in the Black Sea serve no one’s interests,” Erdogan said.

“We cannot accept these attacks under any circumstances, regardless of who carries them out or what justification is offered,” he said, adding, “We call on all parties to act responsibly on this matter.”

Turkiye, which maintains ties with both Moscow and Kyiv, has been angered by the strikes on commercial shipping.

Ankara has sent Russia and Ukraine a proposal to end attacks, but says neither side has acted on it.

Zelenskyy accused Russia of making the situation in the Black Sea difficult and said a significant part of his conversation with Erdogan focused on security there.

“Today, I reached an agreement with President Erdogan to work on the Black Sea grain corridor,” he said.

He said Turkiye supports efforts to ensure safe navigation in the Black Sea and restore normal living conditions.

“We discussed with President Erdogan some ideas and proposals that can help,” Zelenskyy said, thanking the Turkish leader for the dialogue.

Erdogan said talks to restore safe navigation would continue.

“I believe that reaching an agreement on this issue would also give fresh impetus to efforts to secure lasting peace in Ukraine,” he said.

The US is reviewing proposals by Turkiye and India to get grain shipments moving, according to Rubio.

“This is threatening the world for food security and some energy security as well,” Rubio told a news conference in Atlanta, Georgia, following a G20 foreign ministers meeting. “We’d like to achieve it. It doesn’t solve the war, but at least it solves a unique aspect of it.”

Erdogan also welcomed renewed momentum behind efforts to end the Russia-Ukraine war through diplomatic means, pointing in particular to US President Donald Trump’s initiative.

“At this point, we maintain that there can be no losers in a just peace,” he said, adding, “I would like to emphasise that we stand ready to make every possible effort to pave the way for peace”.

Turkiye has hosted several rounds of talks between Russia and Ukraine aimed at a lasting ceasefire and peace deal, which Erdogan said showed that “tangible results can be achieved through diplomacy”.

In a phone call with Trump on Wednesday, Erdogan said Turkiye was ready to support efforts to revive the diplomatic process and end the war, according to the Turkish president’s office.

Last week, the Kremlin said the next round of talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US was planned to resume in November in the United Arab Emirates.

Zelenskyy said he had discussed that format with Erdogan, along with other options, including involving Turkiye, Europe and other partners, as well as the possibility of a meeting in Turkiye.

“Strong decisions are needed for there to be peace,” he said. “And it is necessary at all levels to send signals to Russia that there is no alternative to peace and that support for Ukraine will continue.”

Heading: Iran’s Revolutionary Guard reports three tankers on fire in Strait of Hormuz as talks continue
DNU Summary: The Guard said the vessels used routes Tehran considers unauthorised but did not identify the ships or their crews.
Body:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Friday, Oct. 30, that three oil tankers had encountered incidents while attempting to navigate routes Tehran considers unauthorized in the eastern and western sections of the Strait of Hormuz. All vessels were subsequently stopped in the waterway’s southern waters.

According to Iranian state media, the Guard claimed the tankers had switched off their navigation and positioning systems and were attempting to leave the strait through routes opposed by Tehran, with the support of the U.S. military.

The Guard said the vessels continued sailing despite repeated radio warnings before encountering trouble in what it described as unsafe areas.

It provided no details about the tankers’ identities, their flags, the precise cause of the incidents or the condition of their crews.

The reports came as Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday to continue efforts to broker an agreement between Iran and the United States.

In a separate incident whose possible connection to the Guard’s claims remains unclear, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, or UKMTO, reported that a small boat approached an oil tanker Thursday evening and attached two explosive devices to its hull above the waterline.

The devices detonated, sparking a fire in the engine room and temporarily disabling the vessel.

The Financial Times identified the tanker as the Louise 1.

The incident occurred about 25 nautical miles (46 kilometers) northeast of Khasab, Oman.

UKMTO said the fire had been extinguished, all crew members were safe and no environmental pollution had been reported. The tanker subsequently resumed its voyage toward its next port.

The attack appeared to mark the first reported successful use of limpet mines against a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz since the U.S.-Iran war began in February 2026.

It was not immediately clear who was responsible or whether the attack was connected to the Guard’s latest claims involving two tankers.

Separately, Oman’s Maritime Security Center reported Friday that the Royal Navy of Oman had evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged commercial vessel that came under attack and caught fire about 1.6 nautical miles off the coast of Musandam.

The center said the crew members received necessary medical care but did not identify the vessel or those responsible for the attack.

It remained unclear whether the incident was connected to other reported attacks on tankers in the strait.

The Guard’s latest statements followed claims Thursday, Oct. 29, that three tankers had struck naval mines along the strait’s southern route, triggering explosions and fires.

Iran’s regular military also reported Thursday that another tanker had caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.

According to Agence France-Presse, Iranian officials claimed that all four vessels had been operating in prohibited and unsafe areas.

However, it remained unclear whether the two tankers mentioned in Friday’s Guard statement were additional vessels or were among those involved in the incidents reported Thursday.

Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, reiterated that the Strait of Hormuz’s main shipping lanes had been cleared of Iranian naval mines.

He also claimed that Iran’s navy had been destroyed and that Revolutionary Guard forces were no longer operating in the waterway.

Cooper said U.S. forces remained in the region to keep major shipping routes open and secure.

CENTCOM also rejected a claim made Thursday by the Revolutionary Guard that it had taken control of an American MQM-170 Outlaw drone in the western Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian sources, meanwhile, reported Friday that an American unmanned surface vessel had been destroyed in the eastern Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. military had neither confirmed nor denied that report at the time of publication.

The growing number of maritime incidents comes amid a continuing dispute between Washington and Tehran over the routes used by commercial shipping through the strategic waterway.

Iran has demanded that vessels coordinate their movements with Iranian authorities and use routes closer to the strait’s northern shores. Ships seeking to avoid Iranian control have instead used the southern route.

Diplomatic efforts to prevent another major escalation in the U.S.-Iran war are continuing alongside mounting military tensions in the Strait of Hormuz.

CBS News, citing a source familiar with the negotiations, reported signs of progress and said Iran was expected to respond to a revised proposal from Qatari mediators by the end of the week.

The diplomatic initiative is aimed at preventing a resumption of large-scale U.S. strikes against Iran, a possibility President Donald Trump has repeatedly raised in recent weeks.

Axios reported that Qatari-led mediators were seeking common ground on issues including inspections of Iran’s nuclear facilities and sanctions relief.

However, disagreements persisted over the conditions for formally opening negotiations.

Axios also reported that the United States and Israel were considering options for extensive military strikes against Iran after the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections.

The Associated Press reported Thursday, citing two diplomats, that Washington had warned several regional allies about the possibility of renewed U.S. attacks on Iran and potential Iranian retaliation, although Trump had not made a final decision.

Trump, speaking Friday to a Kansas City radio station, said the war with Iran would end "soon," but did not specify whether that would be achieved through a diplomatic agreement or military action.

The U.S. president reiterated that Washington wanted guarantees that Iran would never acquire a nuclear weapon.

His remarks came as there was still no clear indication that Tehran and Washington had reached an agreement on the conditions for ending the war, while the possibility of renewed large-scale military strikes remained on the table.

Heading: At least four Palestinians killed in Gaza as Israeli attacks continue
DNU Summary: Shelling of the Nuseirat refugee camp killed a teacher, according to al-Awda Hospital.
Body:
Israel carried out several attacks in Gaza, including shelling the Nuseirat refugee camp.

At least four Palestinians in Gaza have been killed as Israel continues to attack the enclave, despite a so-called “ceasefire” that has been in place for over a year.

Israel carried out several attacks in Gaza on Saturday, including shelling the Nuseirat refugee camp, in which Palestinian teacher Diaa Abu al-Rous was killed, al-Awda Hospital confirmed.

Separately, another man, Arafat al-Arair, died after sustaining serious injuries days earlier when Israel struck a vehicle in the Tel al-Hawa neighbourhood, southwest of Gaza City. A medical source at al-Shifa Hospital confirmed his death.

Meanwhile, two girls also died on Saturday from injuries sustained the previous evening when their tent caught fire at a camp for displaced people in al-Mawasi, in Khan Younis. Nasser Medical Complex confirmed their deaths. It is not clear what caused the fire.

At least six Palestinians were killed in Gaza over the past 48 hours, according to the enclave’s Ministry of Health, bringing the number of people killed since the October 2025 ceasefire to 1,580.

In its daily statistical report on Saturday, the ministry said another 26 people were injured over the same period.

The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) warned on Friday that Israeli forces in Gaza were continuing to displace Palestinians and that their actions continued to raise concerns of ethnic cleansing.

The OHCHR said in a statement that Palestinians were increasingly being forced into a shrinking area of the territory, which has been decimated following three years of Israeli siege.

The office said Israeli forces were destroying what remained of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure. The Israeli military is working to expand its control over Gaza’s territory to 70 percent, following an order from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in May.

Reporting from Deir el-Balah, Al Jazeera’s Tareq Abu Azzoum said Israel was targeting civilians as it sought to displace Palestinians from the city.

“We have testimonies from people who have evacuated their homes in the eastern part of Deir el-Balah city, confirming that the Israeli military has adjusted the yellow demarcation line by opening fire on civilians to push them from these areas,” Abu Azzoum said.

Since a nominal “ceasefire” came into effect a year ago, Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,580 Palestinians and injured 5,711 others, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.

Talks aimed at permanently ending Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza under United States President Donald Trump’s peace plan have stalled. Reconstruction efforts have yet to begin amid disputes between Hamas and Israel over the implementation of Trump’s plan.

Hamas says it will not fully disarm until Israel withdraws entirely from Gaza. However, Israel maintains it will not leave the territory until Hamas forfeits its weapons.

Heading: Aliyev to skip Turkey-led summit for first time in more than a decade amid growing tension
DNU Summary: Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov will represent Azerbaijan at the Organisation of Turkic States meeting.
Body:
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev will skip the upcoming summit of the Organisation of Turkic States (OTS) in Turkey amid growing tensions between Baku and Ankara following a series of political disagreements. It is the first time in almost 15 years of the OTS that Aliyev will not attend an official summit.

Although Azerbaijani officials have attributed his absence to a busy schedule, the decision comes as relations between the two countries have come under increasing strain following a dispute over hijab restrictions in Azerbaijani schools, public criticism by Turkish officials, and a series of increasingly critical statements in pro-government media on both sides.

Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov will represent Azerbaijan at the summit. Other Azerbaijani representatives are also expected to attend events held on the sidelines of the meeting.

On Friday, Aliyev is expected to attend the awards ceremony for finalists of the FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival in Baku. The tournament's final match and official closing ceremony are also scheduled for that day.

Foreign Minister Bayramov will lead the Azerbaijani delegation at the OTS summit.

Discord between the two allies emerged publicly after schoolgirls wearing hijabs were prevented from entering schools in Azerbaijan after new legislation was introduced.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral and several ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) lawmakers criticised the restrictions.

Azerbaijan's ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), meanwhile, described their statements as interference in the country’s internal affairs.

Saral left his position on 26 October with Turkish media reports having linked his departure to the discord between Baku and Ankara that his statements contributed to.

Another potential point of divergence between Baku and Ankara concerns the selection of the next UN Secretary-General.Azerbaijan's Foreign Ministry has welcomed the United Arab Emirates’ initiative to nominate Lana Nusseibeh for the position.

Turkey, meanwhile, has put forward former Foreign Minister Feridun Sinirlioğlu as its candidate.

Following confirmation that Aliyev would not travel to Turkey, several pro-government Azerbaijani media outlets published analyses discussing the reasons behind his absence.

An analysis published by the pro-government APA, titled Why did President Ilham Aliyev not travel to Turkey?, accused circles in Turkey of conducting an anti-Azerbaijani campaign and described Erdoğan's phone call to Aliyev as a belated gesture. The article also stressed that diplomacy was based on reciprocity.

The analysis recalled that Erdoğan had also skipped the informal OTS summit held in Shusha in 2024, where Turkey was represented by Vice-President Cevdet Yılmaz. Erdoğan attended the quarter-final match between Turkey and the Netherlands at the UEFA European Championship in Berlin on the same day.

Erdoğan also did not attend the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA), held in Baku on 15 October this year. Turkey was represented by Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan.

Another pro-government outlet, Trend.az, published a similar analysis, attributing Aliyev’s absence to what it described as a campaign against Azerbaijan and its president in Turkey. The article also argued that such actions were more commonly expected from Iran than from Turkey.

Independent Azerbaijani journalists and media outlets operating outside the country have documented the increase in tension.

According to the outlet Open Azerbaijan, citing an unnamed source, Azerbaijani Parliament Speaker Sahiba Gafarova purportedly instructed MPs not to attend official events organised by the Turkish Embassy in Baku. The source also alleged that Gafarova had instructed MPs to reduce their contacts with Turkish officials.

Separately, journalist Ganimat Zahid, who lives in France, wrote on Facebook that Azerbaijani MPs with the ruling party YAP did not attend an official reception organised by the Turkish Embassy at Gulustan Palace in Baku to mark Turkey's Republic Day, as they were apparently prohibited from doing so.

He said that MPs belonging to other pro-government parties and those not affiliated with YAP were not subject to the same restrictions, which — according to him — explained their attendance.

Zahid also claimed that television channels had been instructed not to attend the reception or broadcast reports from the event.

According to his account, Azerbaijan was represented by the Minister of Digital Development and Transport, Rashad Nabiyev, who is not affiliated with any political party and left the venue shortly after delivering a speech.

The Azerbaijani authorities have not publicly confirmed these reported restrictions.

The dispute has also attracted attention in Turkey, where several media outlets have questioned Aliyev's decision not to attend the Ankara summit.

The Turkish newspaper Sözcü published an article asking why Aliyev had not travelled to Ankara despite Erdoğan personally calling and inviting him. Another Turkish outlet, Yeniçağ, questioned whether the dispute could be explained solely by the controversy surrounding hijab restrictions in Azerbaijani schools.

Meanwhile, the Azerbaijani outlet Time TV suggested that the disagreement stemmed from problems between the two countries' leaders. It also argued that Aliyev might have avoided the visit out of concern that he could face public protests in Turkey over the hijab restrictions.

Speaking at the summit on Friday, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said there was no room for division in the family photo of Turkic states. He also said Turkey had assumed the OTS chairmanship from Azerbaijan and expressed his intention to advance cooperation within the organisation in several areas.

Erdoğan said the summit's theme had been set as ‘Turkey's Century: Unity in Language, Thought, and Action’.

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this article incorrectly said it was the first time that President Ilham Aliyev had skipped an OTS summit in its 17-year history. Aliyev did not attend the 2012 summit, which was instead attended by then-Prime Minister Artur Rasizade.

Rafiq Shahbazov is a journalist based in Tbilisi, covering political and social developments in Azerbaijan, as well as issues affecting ethnic Azerbaijanis in the region. He has worked with independent media outlets. His work focuses on human rights, environmental issues, and pressure on journalists and civil society.

Heading: Georgia, Azerbaijan Hold Intergovernmental Meeting, Talk ‘Speeding Up’ Border Process
DNU Summary: Their prime ministers met in Tbilisi and discussed trade, energy and the shared border near David Gareji.
Body:
Georgia and Azerbaijan signed documents, discussed cooperation, and agreed to speed up the border demarcation and delimitation process as officials from the two countries held the 11th meeting of the Georgia-Azerbaijan Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation on October 30 in Tbilisi.

The meeting, co-chaired by Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and visiting Azerbaijani Prime Minister Ali Asadov, focused on trade, energy cooperation, infrastructure, and Middle Corridor-related projects. Kobakhidze also told the journalists later that the two sides had agreed to accelerate the process of demarcating and delimiting their shared border, including the area around the historic David Gareji Monastery complex.

Following the meeting, Kobakhidze and Asadov signed the protocol of its 11th session, while the officials from the two countries also signed “an agreement on the practical operation of the joint Georgia-Azerbaijan international road border crossing point, Silk Road-Ipek Yolu, as well as memoranda of understanding on cooperation in the fields of veterinary services and plant protection,” according to the Georgian government’s press release.

Kobakhidze also held a separate meeting with Asadov, during which they discussed bilateral strategic partnership, cooperation across various sectors, as well as “the prospects for the Middle Corridor and the particularly important role of the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars (BTK) railway in enhancing regional transport connectivity.”

According to the Georgian Dream government’s press service, officials from the two countries reviewed progress in trade and economic cooperation over recent years and discussed plans, with attention devoted to the Middle Corridor, “major infrastructure projects underway in Georgia, the successful partnership in the energy sector and opportunities for implementing new joint initiatives.”

The press service cited Kobakhidze as saying that “for centuries, our peoples have lived side by side, respecting each other’s traditions and national interests. It is precisely this mutual respect that has been and continues to be the solid foundation of our partnership.”

Kobakhidze noted that the two countries’ strategic partnership is reflected in their high-level political dialogue, pointing to Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Georgia in April, which, he said, “once again reaffirmed our mutual interest in further developing and deepening bilateral relations.”

He also addressed the “ongoing geopolitical developments in the region,” highlighting that Georgia has “always been a strong advocate of peaceful coexistence and dialogue in the region.”

Kobakhidze described Azerbaijan as “among Georgia’s largest trading partners,” saying the objective is to “build on the progress achieved, including by better utilizing the export potential of Georgian products, further diversifying trade relations and providing additional incentives for investment.”

He highlighted the Middle Corridor project, saying it’s “our shared objective” to “further increase the capacity, efficiency and competitiveness of this route.”

To achieve this goal, Kobakhidze said Georgia is implementing “large-scale infrastructure projects,” including the East-West Highway, the modernization and expansion of Georgian Railway, the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars (BTK) railway, the Anaklia Deep Sea Port and the new Tbilisi International Airport.

On energy cooperation, he highlighted the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) oil pipeline, the Baku-Tbilisi-Erzurum gas pipeline, the Baku-Supsa oil pipeline and the Southern Gas Corridor, saying these projects “have for many years facilitated the reliable transit of energy resources while contributing to regional and European energy security.”

He also noted that, together with Azerbaijan, Romania and Hungary, “Georgia is participating in the development of the Green Energy Corridor, an initiative aimed at facilitating the transmission of renewable energy and strengthening the integration of the South Caucasus with the European energy market.”

Kobakhidze added that the agenda of bilateral relations “also encompasses defense, culture, education, agriculture, healthcare, tourism and customs cooperation,” saying Georgia stood ready to strengthen existing ties and facilitate new joint initiatives.

The press release also included remarks by Azerbaijani Prime Minister Ali Asadov, who noted that the strategic partnership had entered “a qualitatively new phase” in recent years, also highlighting Aliyev’s visit to Tbilisi and Kobakhidze’s visit to Baku in May.

He described Georgia as one of Azerbaijan’s “key trading partners,” noting that during “the first nine months of this year, bilateral trade volumes increased by over 40%, reaching 1 billion USD compared with the corresponding period of the previous year.”

“Our cooperation in the field of investment is also demonstrating very positive momentum. Azerbaijan has invested approximately 4 billion USD in Georgia,” he said.

On major infrastructure and energy projects, Asadov highlighted the Southern Gas Corridor, saying it plays a particularly important role in “ensuring energy security in the region and Europe.” He also noted that cooperation in the electricity sector is developing successfully and that the two countries are working on the Green Energy Corridor project to Europe.

He pointed to the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway and the increase in its capacity to five million tonnes, describing it as the “result of our successful joint efforts.”

Asadov also highlighted cultural and humanitarian cooperation, expressing hope that “construction of the new building of the Heydar Aliyev Tbilisi State Professional Azerbaijani Drama Theatre will begin in the near future.”

“The Azerbaijani and Georgian communities residing in our respective countries play a particularly important role in strengthening bilateral relations,” he was cited as saying. “Providing education in their native languages and the achievements of the relevant schools contribute to deepening the ties between our peoples.”

Speaking to the media following the meetings, Kobakhidze said the two sides “touched on the issue of border demarcation and delimitation,” including Davit Gareji Monastery and “the corresponding territory.”

According to Kobakhidze, the Georgian side “expressed hope that work on border demarcation and delimitation will continue at a very fast pace,” noting that “there has been no change over the past many years in terms of border demarcation and delimitation, and we need rapid progress.”

Kobakhidze added that they expressed that request to the Azerbaijani side, “to which we received a very friendly response,” and that “we agreed that we will speed up the processes related to border demarcation and delimitation.”

He noted that “there are approximately 15 such sections, and we need to work very actively on all fifteen. The main thing is to resolve the issue in principle, and for that, it is essential to complete the demarcation and delimitation process and to move forward in this direction, and that is exactly what we discussed today.”

Heading: Kobakhidze again says Tbilisi ‘ready’ to restore US-Georgia ties after chargé d’affaires meeting
DNU Summary: Relations have been effectively frozen since the Biden administration, and Washington has had no ambassador in Tbilisi since July 2025.
Body:
Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze again said Tbilisi is ready to ‘restore’ ties with the US after meeting the newly appointed US Chargé d’Affaires Courtney Austrian on Thursday. The meeting comes amidst a now yearslong effective freeze in Georgia–US relations which began under the administration of former President Joe Biden and has continued into President Donald Trump’s term.

The US has had no ambassador to Georgia since the previous US ambassador, Robin Dunnigan, retired and left Georgia in July 2025. At the end of her term, Dunnigan said that Georgian Dream had sent a private letter to Trump that was ‘threatening, insulting, [and] unserious’.

She did not reveal the specifics of the letter.

During the meeting between Kobakhidze and Austrian, described by the US Embassy as ‘introductory’, the two parties discussed Georgia-US relations.

‘The Prime Minister once again confirmed that Georgia is ready to restore the strategic partnership with the USA from a clean sheet. Irakli Kobakhidze emphasised the important role of acting ambassador in this process’, the Georgian government said, regarding the meeting with Austrian, who was appointed in September 2026.

In August, Kobakhidze met the interim US chargé d’affaires Amy Diaz to discuss Georgia-US relations.

The meetings come amid a decline in US–Georgia relations. Washington suspended the US–Georgia Strategic Partnership mechanism in November 2024, after Georgian Dream announced it would suspend Georgia’s EU accession process until 2028.

The US State Department said at the time that Georgian Dream’s actions had violated the core principles of the strategic partnership, and condemned, what it called, the excessive use of force against protesters.

The US had already taken several measures against the Georgian government in the previous year including suspending more than $95 million in assistance to the government and imposing visa restrictions on individuals accused of undermining democracy.

In December 2024, the US Treasury Department sanctioned Georgian Dream founder and honorary chair Bidzina Ivanishvili under an executive order targeting Russia-related activities.

Georgian Dream leaders had repeatedly said that Trump’s return to the White House would lead to a change in US policy towards Georgia. However, the sanctions imposed by Washington were not lifted following his election.

In early August, the US decided to make its visa bond programme for Georgians permanent. The rules, introduced at the start of the year, oblige Georgians to post a bond of up to $20,000 to obtain a tourist or business visa Georgia is the only European country to be subject to the scheme and is also the only state in the region to be included in a list of ‘high-risk’ countries the US associates with overstays.

Aslan is a Georgian–Azerbaijani student expanding the age gap at OC Media as an intern. He enjoys working out 6–7 days a week and keeping up with Rustaveli Avenue’s renovation.

Heading: More than 290 arrested in France as some weekend protests turn violent
DNU Summary: The interior ministry counted 320,000 demonstrators nationwide, including 70,000 in Paris.
Body:
Protests continue across France as 320,000 people take to the streets over rising living costs and poor school conditions for a third consecutive weekend, with clashes reported in several cities.

A number of clashes have been reported between protesters and police in several French cities on Saturday as hundreds of thousands of people again took to the streets nationwide to protest the rising cost of living and conditions in schools.

The French Interior Ministry said 320,000 people had participated in demonstrations across the country, including 70,000 in Paris.

"The marches proceeded smoothly within the framework of the declared demonstrations," the ministry said, while noting that "radical elements" in several cities, including Bordeaux, Toulouse and Marseille, had attempted to enter city centres "with the aim of carrying out vandalism and looting."

In Marseille, footage showed fires burning in the streets as firefighters responded. Clashes with police were also reported in Rennes and Toulouse.

After a largely peaceful start to the day, police fired tear gas in Paris and Lyon in the late afternoon, according to French media reports and live broadcast footage. Tensions in the capital escalated as demonstrators reached the end of their march on the city's southern outskirts.

Footage aired by BFMTV showed fireworks exploding and incendiary devices being thrown at officers in riot gear, with several officers caught in the flames.

Paris police carried out more than 1,200 checks at railway stations and nearby areas early on Saturday to identify potential troublemakers, the city's police prefecture said.

The checks aimed to prevent demonstrators from bringing fireworks, knives and other prohibited items to the marches.

Police also deployed "all available resources" in the air to monitor security throughout the day, the prefecture said. An official order authorized camera-equipped drones to capture and transmit live images of the situation across the capital.

More than 290 arrests were made on Saturday across France, according to police.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned earlier Saturday that the demonstrations posed a "very high risk," citing calls for looting and rioting.

Around 70,000 police officers and other security personnel were deployedacross the country to maintain order during the protests.

Authorities also feared that Halloween celebrations could give people an opportunity to conceal their identities while committing offenses.

Amid concerns over attacks on public buildings and looting, officials ordered protest routes in Paris and other cities to be moved away from city centers.

Many shops and businesses responded by boarding up their windows and taking other precautions. Curfews and other restrictions were also imposed in several cities, including measures targeting specific areas and minors.

A similarly large security deployment last weekend largely prevented a repeat of the violence and destruction seen during the October 17 protests.

Young people have been taking to the streets for weeks to protest inadequate staffing and equipment in schools. Since mid-October, other groups have joined the demonstrations, mainly over the rising cost of living.

Trade unions, school and student organizations, and the grassroots Yellow Vest movement, which first rose to prominence in France in 2018, called for Saturday's protests.

Heading: Polish president Nawrocki pushes his way into top court amid rule-of-law tussle
DNU Summary: He entered the Constitutional Tribunal amid a dispute over the appointment of its acting president.
Body:
Karol Nawrocki made his way through protesters around midnight in the latest escalation of his conflict with Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

WARSAW — Polish President Karol Nawrocki forced his way into the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw shortly after midnight on Saturday, in the latest escalation of the rule-of-law tussle between the PiS-allied president and Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

A video published overnight showed Nawrocki pushing through people gathered at the court’s entrance, including Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, the judge whose disputed nomination as the court’s acting president triggered the crisis on Friday.

Another judge of the top court, Maciej Berek, accused the president of physically confronting Korwin-Piotrowska. Presidential aide Rafał Leśkiewicz claimed it was the judges, whom he called “usurpers,” who had obstructed and manhandled Nawrocki.

Inside, Nawrocki told Korwin-Piotrowska and other judges that were recently elected by Tusk’s parliamentary majority: “You are not judges [of the Tribunal].”

The confrontation marked a dramatic escalation in the struggle between Nawrocki and Tusk’s government over how to reverse judicial changes introduced under the former nationalist Law and Justice (PiS) government.

Korwin-Piotrowska suspended the court’s president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy Bartłomiej Sochański — both named by PiS and seen as loyalists — claiming authority to take over the court’s management. Święczkowski rejected the move.

In a statement issued around 5 a.m., Nawrocki accused the government of “forcibly seizing a constitutional institution”, demanded that police leave the court grounds and summoned emergency consultations with parliamentary parties for Saturday, citing a “threat to Poland’s internal security.”

Police remain deployed outside the tribunal, where PiS supporters had staged an anti-government protest camp for weeks.

The broader dispute stems from Tusk’s efforts to reverse controversial moves by former PiS governments to fill the court with judges aligned with the nationalist party. These efforts have met stiff resistance from PiS and Nawrocki, who refused to swear in some judges elected by the Tusk-led parliamentary majority.

The judges subsequently took oaths in parliament, in a ceremony Nawrocki considers null and void, while Święczkowski barred them from hearing cases.

Heading: Starmer says UK must get closer to Europe as US relationship changes
DNU Summary: The former prime minister warned European leaders about Russia and said relations with Washington were unlikely to reset soon.
Body:
The UK and other European nations must draw closer together as the US becomes a less-reliable partner, Keir Starmer has said in his first significant political intervention since leaving No 10.

The former prime minister warned European leaders of the threat posed by Russia, among others, and said the shift in relations with Washington during Donald Trump’s presidency was not likely to reset once he leaves the Oval Office. He accused them of being caught out by these new realities twice already.

“A stronger Europe is vital and the UK must be at the heart of it,” Starmer told an audience at the British Irish Chamber of Commerce on Friday. “Europe has twice been caught asleep, failing to anticipate and prepare for predictable events.

“First, when Russia’s attack on Ukraine exposed longstanding European weaknesses on defence and security, and second, when President Trump made clear, once and for all, that the US will no longer bankroll our European security. We have to catch up.”

Starmer had called for closer European ties before stepping down as prime minister in July. Three months earlier, amid Trump’s war with Iran and his threats to withdraw from Nato, Starmer said Europe represented a “partnership for a dangerous world we must navigate together”.

He said those ties should go further than just defence, adding that Brexit had done “deep damage” to the UK economy, and that he wanted to be “more ambitious”, including pursuing “closer economic cooperation [and] closer security cooperation”.

Starmer spoke after spending time in Dublin meeting senior business leaders and politicians, including the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, with whom he established the annual UK-Ireland summit.

“I will say here what I have said to European leaders. This is about responding to a permanent change of affairs, not an aberration of the Trump presidency. Things will not go back to the way they were before.

“That doesn’t mean the US relationship is no longer important. On the contrary, the military, security and intelligence alliance is far too strong for that. But it does mean enabling Europe to take on far more responsibility for its own defence and security.”

His comments reflect a growing consensus on the left of UK politics that closer ties with Europe are essential to ensure economic and military security. Soon after taking office as Starmer’s successor, Andy Burnham said that he intended to be “bolder” about closer ties with the EU.

Next month, Burnham will attend a crucial EU-UK summit where new agreements on food standards, energy and youth mobility will be the main focus.

Burnham has also said he wants a public debate on how the UK could move to a closer relationship with the EU after the next election. At a meeting of European defence ministers in Paris this week, the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said that they were “united and unwavering” in support for Ukraine in the face of Russian hostility.

Starmer said: “We need to build up pan-European cooperation and coordination on defence and security – a common security framework as much as a common market. The EU is changing to respond to that, but it cannot be the EU alone when Europe’s periphery is core to its defence.

“Britain must be central to that project. We are one of two nuclear powers. We are a leading Nato member. We have a viable next-generation fighter jet programme. And we are pledged to work alongside European allies to guarantee security in Ukraine.

“Ireland and the UK stand side by side in the coalition of the willing and with Ukraine, working together to guarantee and shape the security of our continent. I hope and believe that Britain’s relationship with its friends and allies can and should be strengthened by this urgent and common security project.”

Heading: U.S. Embassy Warns of Potential 'Mass Casualty Event' in Moscow
DNU Summary: The embassy cited a threat at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve and said it was coordinating with Russian authorities.
Body:
The United States Embassy in Moscow on Saturday issued an urgent security alert, warning of a potential mass casualty event in the Russian capital.

“The U.S. Embassy in Moscow is aware of a credible threat of a mass casualty event TODAY October 31, at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve in Moscow at Dolskaya Ulitsa 1, Moscow, Russia 11569. The U.S. government is coordinating with appropriate Russian authorities on a response,” the statement said.

The statement also warned people to avoid the area and take measures to ensure personal safety.

Later on Saturday, state media reported that the Federal Security Service (FSB) had received information from the U.S. regarding the potential terrorist attack.

“We have received information from U.S. partners regarding plans for a terrorist attack in Moscow. We are taking appropriate action,” the FSB told state media.

Tsaritsyno was evacuated Saturday while musician Lilia Pechenkina was playing a concert. “Just as I was playing the last piece in the program, an evacuation announcement came over the loudspeaker,” Pechenkina told news outlet Ostorozhno, Novosti!.

The Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve has been closed for “technical reasons,” a journalist from Ostorozhno, Novosti! was told by security.

Around 50 law enforcement officers have been dispatched to the area, and police vehicles are patrolling the perimeter, the Baza Telegram channel, which allegedly has ties to the Russian security services, reported.

In 2024, the U.S. warned Moscow of an impending terrorist threat ahead of the March 22 Crocus City Hall attack, which left 145 people dead and hundreds more wounded.

At the time, Russian spy chief Sergei Naryshkin called the information “too general.”

“The Federal Security Service [FSB] received some information from the U.S. intelligence services that such a thing was unfortunately possible. But as our Russian colleagues said, the information was too general and did not allow us to fully identify those who committed this terrible crime,” he said.

Heading: They strangled us, says founder of Russian newspaper shut under pressure from authorities
DNU Summary: Novaya Gazeta says it is being evicted from its long-time offices and blocked from receiving donations.
Body:
At the editorial offices of Novaya Gazeta, they are packing up and shutting down.

Everywhere I look there are cardboard boxes and plastic bags. Everything must go.

For thirty years this has been Russia's most prominent independent newspaper, featuring investigative journalism fiercely critical of those in power.

Now Novaya Gazeta is being evicted from its home of three decades. The paper also says it's been blocked from receiving donations.

It's accusing the Russian authorities of killing it off.

"There are different ways to commit murder," journalist and co-founder of the paper Dmitry Muratov tells me. "They chose to strangle us."

"First, they blocked our websites and banned the paper edition. Then they revoked our media licence. One by one we were declared 'foreign agents', and our journalists were attacked.

"Now we can't earn any more money. The banks are refusing to accept donations from our readers. In our country there are political repressions going on. Those have reached us."

In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".

The award didn't stop the Russian authorities from designating him a 'foreign agent' in 2023. The label is often used to punish critics of the government.

Over the years Novaya Gazeta had developed a reputation for fearless investigative reporting on subjects such as corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power by officials and bureaucrats - dangerous topics in Russia.

The paper says that six colleagues were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty". Those journalists include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block twenty years ago this month. She had written extensively on the wars in Chechnya.

As I walk down a corridor, I spot the office Anna had used. Following her killing, the room and all the items in it were preserved and became a museum in her memory. Since the eviction order, most of the objects have already been removed. All that's left is the desk and, lying on top, a portrait of Anna.

In a statement on its website announcing the closure, Novaya Gazeta launched a stinging attack on the Russian authorities.

"They've killed us," it starts. "The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian special services have forced the paper to stop its work."

The publication claims it is the victim of "a coordinated act" and blames "the repressive state apparatus".

"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country and their protection has been equated to a crime… The courts have been destroyed along with the law. Having personal convictions is now state treason."

Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the pressure on independent journalism and independent Russian journalists has been growing.

Soon after the start of what the Kremlin calls the 'special military operation', new laws were adopted in Russia. Their aim: to punish dissent and silence criticism of the war and of those in power.

Earlier this year there was a police search of Novaya Gazeta's editorial office. A veteran investigative journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested and charged with "unlawful access to computerised information".

In connection with the case the newspaper's current editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov was recently taken in for police questioning and his home was searched.

Despite increasing pressure, Novaya Gazeta managed to continue operating, albeit in a reduced form. Loyal readers used VPNs, virtual private networks, to circumvent official blocking of the website. But the loss of its licence and other restrictions were a major blow to the publication.

How does Dmitry Muratov view the future?

"We are in the middle of a terrible catastrophe," Mr Muratov tells me. "Different dictatorships in the world seek chaos. They use chaos to rule their countries and peoples and to strengthen their personal power.

"I don't know what will happen next. I do know that we will do everything to stay true to our values: the human right to life. Human rights override the rights of states."

Novaya Gazeta's demise is very much the end of an era.

In an increasingly authoritarian Russia, it's also a sign of the times.

Heading: North Korea warns South Korea with ballistic missiles as Seoul calls for talks to ease border tensions
DNU Summary: South Korea said roughly a dozen missiles were launched from Wonsan and travelled about 250 kilometres.
Body:
North Korea fired around a dozen short-range ballistic missiles towards the sea on Thursday, South Korea’s military said, a day after Seoul renewed its call for talks to prevent accidental clashes along their heavily fortified border.

The missiles were launched from the eastern coastal area of Wonsan at about 12.30pm local time and travelled around 250 kilometres, according to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff.

South Korea said it had stepped up surveillance for further launches and was sharing information with the United States and Japan.

Seoul proposed military talks on 23 October to jointly verify the location of the Military Demarcation Line, which separates the two Koreas, restore military communication lines and agree measures to prevent accidental clashes.

Unification Minister Chung Dong-young renewed the appeal on Wednesday in an address read on his behalf at a forum in Goyang, near Seoul.

“South and North Korea should align their positions on the MDL through dialogue,” Chung said, calling for communication channels to be restored so the area could be managed peacefully.

North Korea has not responded to the talks proposal.

The offer follows landmine explosions in the Demilitarised Zone on 21 September that injured three South Korean soldiers, two of them seriously.

Seoul accused North Korean troops of planting the mines south of the demarcation line. North Korea denied responsibility and accused the South of fabricating the incident in a letter to the UN Security Council.

The US-led United Nations Command, which oversees the armistice, said a joint investigation with South Korea had identified an active North Korean mine south of the line and determined that an armistice violation had occurred.

North Korean troops have been reinforcing the border with roads, fences and landmines. South Korea says they have repeatedly crossed the demarcation line during the work, prompting warning broadcasts and warning shots.

Seoul says differing interpretations of the boundary could lead to accidental clashes. Many of the markers installed under the 1953 armistice have deteriorated or disappeared, with only about 200 of the original 1,292 still identifiable, according to Yonhap.

Direct military communication between the two Koreas remains suspended, although the command maintains a separate channel with the North Korean military.

Heading: Canada and EU announce new alliance open to like-minded countries
DNU Summary: Mark Carney and Ursula von der Leyen announced the Alliance for the Future during talks in Montreal.
Body:
Canada and Europe have announced a new alliance of like-minded nations to serve as both a “protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive” and a powerful hedge against the unpredictable nature of geopolitics, while welcoming other countries to join.

Speaking to reporters on Friday from Montreal, the prime minister, Mark Carney, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, called the new partnership the Alliance for the Future and said the “deepest possible partnership between Canada and the 27-member bloc had the potential to offer unprecedented stability and opportunity”.

“Our societies have been shaken by new storms,” Carney told reporters, referring to the damaging effects of the climate emergency but also the “erosion of democratic norms” and “the weaponization of trade”.

As they concluded their two-day summit, Canada agreed to contribute to a €90bn support loan for Ukraine. Leaders also said future discussions would lead to a more integrated market worth tens of billions of dollars, reduced trade and travel restrictions, and new educational opportunities for both sides.

While a trade war between Canada and the United States has seen Carney go hunting for new geopolitical partners, an over-reliance on American companies – especially for defence – has also given Canada pause.

Last week, Elon Musk throttled the speeds of Starlink and Starshield over Ukraine in mid-October, severely disrupting Ukrainian military and defense operations.

Carney has repeatedly raised the concern that Canada’s defense technologies could be at the whim of political actors or companies with opposing interests. Musk, a dual Canadian citizen, is a critic of Canada’s governing Liberal party and has advocated for provinces to separate.

Carney pointed to a planned merger between the Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere Inc and Germany’s Aleph Alpha GmbH as a step to lessening reliance on American AI giants. The tie-up will see the newly formed company have dual headquarters in Berlin and Toronto, and Canada’s federal government has announced a stake in Cohere worth up to C$1.6bn.

“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know, or by whom we don’t trust,” Carney said on Thursday.

Brussels and Ottawa also announced an agreement on Friday that would bringing Canada into Europe’s supercomputing network, giving Canadian access to European machines to train AI models.

In addition to lofty promises of helping to reshape the global order, or giving safe harbour to like-minded nations looking to weather uncertainty, Canadian and EU leaders also pitched their new, deeper relationship as one that addressed key sources of anxiety for residents, including the cost of living.

“When trade becomes a tool of economic pressure, it’s the families that pay the price, from the supermarket shelf to the cost of a new car,” Von der Leyen said, noting that previously trusted suppliers of energy, critical minerals or semiconductors “are increasingly turned into instruments of pressure”.

“More competition, more choice,” Carney said earlier in the day, suggesting the alliance could find ways to build certainty around supply chains and “withstand shocks, together”.

The leaders once again brought up the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member. The designation is uncharted territory, said Von der Leyen, who added: “We have the ambition, trust, and creativity to shape it together.

“This [associate membership] is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”

While the leaders committed to the idea of associate membership, they said a clearer scope of the role would come at a 2027 summit. Some EU members had bristled at the idea of Canada being given a legally meaningless designation that they fear confuses other nations looking for membership. Germany and other states had worked behind the scenes to remove the phrase from a draft of the summit statement. But Von der Leyen, who first floated the term, and Carney both again referred to “associate membership” at the summit.

European Council president Antonio Costa, meanwhile, said earlier that Canada was “by far the most European of the non-European countries”, a sentiment that reflected a belief that despite geography, there was a collective sense of shared values.

Costa said the two sides would pursue “the most closer, the most deepest, the most stronger association ever between European Union and a non-European country”.

Still, the mere fact of the summit has caused friction in the province of Quebec, where the separatist Parti Québécois was recently elected to a minority government. The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, skipped the event after Ottawa’s refusal to let him speak publicly at it.

“The federal government would have us believe that the premier of Quebec being granted permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence for representing Quebec’s interests,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote in a social media post earlier in the week.

He said an invitation to sit at the head table was the federal government asking Quebec “to get back in line, with the vassalization and invisibilization of Quebec which that implies, in exchange for obtaining better seats to watch the party”.

Heading: UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara to expire amid US, Russia vetoes
DNU Summary: The Security Council failed to renew MINURSO after Washington and Moscow vetoed each other’s draft resolutions.
Body:
The mandate of the UN peacekeeping force in Western Sahara will expire on October 31. The UN Security Council could not agree on a resolution to extend the mission.

The fate of the United Nations peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara has been left in a limbo after Russia and the United States vetoed each other's draft resolutions on extending the mission that is over three decades long — just one day before the mandate expires.

The peacekeeping mission, known as MINURSO, was established in 1991 to oversee a settlement plan and ceasefire between Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front in a territorial dispute spanning half a century.

Morocco considers Western Sahara, a mineral-rich former Spanish colony, as its territory,

The Polisario Front, which is supported by Algeria and represents the indigenous Sahrawi people, seeks to establish an independent state called the Sahrawi Republic.

On Friday, the US tabled a draft resolution at the UN Security Council (UNSC) that would have extended the mandate for one year, while making a Moroccan autonomy plan for Western Sahara the only basis for negotiations to settle the conflict, and cutting the mission's military component.

Last year, the UNSC backed Morocco's autonomy proposal as the "most feasible" solution for the disputed territory.

Friday's failed US draft resolution would have gone further and rebranded the peacekeeping force from MINURSO to MINUSO, dropping the 'R' which refers to referendum on the territory's self-determination.

The US proposal was vetoed by Russia, which slammed it as a "unilateral approach." A total of 11 of the 15 UNSC members voted in its favor and three abstained.

"We stress the fact that the Security Council cannot automatically pre-determine matters relating to sovereignty," Russia's permanent representative to the UN, Vassily Nebenzia, said.

"The Security Council must not give a blessing to such a one-sided approach. Therefore we were compelled to block the adoption of ⁠the draft," ​he added.

The US, with its own veto, then blocked a Russian draft that proposed renewing the mission's mandate for another year while preserving the same terms as before.

"Unfortunately, some members of this Council have used their veto to preserve the letter 'R' for referendum in the mission's name, even though the United Nations has not been preparing to hold such a vote for decades," the US representative to the United Nations, Michael Waltz, said after the vote.

Morocco's royal palace welcomed the failure to renew the peacekeeping mission and said that this "should mark the end of the Security Council's involvement and the removal of this issue from its agenda."

The Polisario Front's UN representative, Sidi Omar, thanked Russia for vetoing the US resolution that he said "would have undermined the free exercise by the Sahrawi people of their inalienable right to self-determination and independence."

Heading: G20 foreign ministers end Atlanta meeting without consensus on key issues
DNU Summary: The group issued a chair’s statement instead of a joint communiqué after divisions over the war in Ukraine.
Body:
ATLANTA (AP) — Top diplomats from the Group of 20 largest world economies wrapped up two days of talks Saturday without reaching consensus on several critical global security issues after divisions, notably over Russia's war with Ukraine, visibly overshadowed the start of the Atlanta meeting and impacted its outcome, too.

As a result, the group did not release a joint communique but relied on a chairman's statement summarizing the talks that Secretary of State Marco Rubio released after the meetings closed.

WATCH: Rubio welcomes G20 foreign ministers to Atlanta at 'critical moment'

That statement made no mention of any agreements reached. Rather, it referred to a list of priorities, from energy and food security to freedom of navigation, that G20 members determined were important to solve.

"I wouldn't pretend to you today that we are close to finding universally accepted solutions to these problems," Rubio told reporters at a news conference marking the end of the meetings.

"But," he said, "I do think that among the G-20 represented here are countries that are working together to solve some of them, particularly in the realm of supply chains and critical minerals."

Rubio had said the first day of the session was "very productive." On Saturday, he hosted sideline talks with his counterparts from Australia, India and Japan before leading the final G20 event that focused on freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Red, Black and South China seas.

"I made clear to our partners that secure supply chains are essential for growth," Rubio said in a social media post on X. "Critical trade routes including the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb Strait must remain secure and open to commerce. And we must continue to strengthen and expand critical mineral supply chains to protect our future."

At a reception for G20 participants Friday night, Rubio sounded optimistic. "Together, I think that we are mapping a vibrant, dynamic, and bold economic future, one that will pioneer new horizons for the entire world," he said.

Rubio had opened the talks Friday with an appeal for unity, but then canceled the traditional group photo of the foreign ministers. European diplomats objected to the inclusion of Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and threatened to boycott or walk out of the snapshot.

Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski, who was representing his country for the first time as a guest at a G20 meeting, said he was not surprised by the failure to reach consensus. "We have wars going on, and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it's very difficult to agree on a common line," he said.

Other participants in the meetings, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the private talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month's summit of G20 leaders hosted by President Donald Trump in Florida a success.

These diplomats said a chairman's statement had long been the plan because of the deep differences among the attendees, including over the Russia-Ukraine war, the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, U.S. tariffs and Chinese moves in the South China Sea. All have contributed to spikes in the global cost of fuel as well as uncertainty about trade.

They described the opening session as cordial but said Russia's position on Ukraine was unyielding — as was its opposition to Poland's membership in the G20. They said the disagreements also included the Trump administration's decision not to invite G20 member South Africa over the objections of others.

Disagreements between even like-minded partners within the G20 were also on display. A joint statement released after Rubio's talks with the Asia-Pacific ministers referred six times to the importance of "Super Intelligence (SI)(asterisk)" in driving economic growth.

The six asterisks led to a footnote making clear that "in Australia, India, and Japan, 'Super Intelligence' refers to 'artificial intelligence." Trump renamed "artificial intelligence" at the U.N. General Assembly in September, saying the phrase sounded fake, and ordered the U.S. government to refer to it as "Super Intelligence." No other country has taken such a step.

Before the meeting began, some G20 countries had expressed concern that the U.S. invited Russia during its heightened attacks on Ukraine, especially after Trump pushed ties with Ukraine to new lows by waiving fresh sanctions on Moscow and temporarily limiting logistical and intelligence assistance.

The State Department, however, announced Friday that it had approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot air defense interceptors for Ukraine.

Rubio defended the decision to invite Lavrov to Atlanta and Putin to the summit, saying it would be impossible to peacefully resolve the crisis without speaking to both sides. And yet he offered a sober assessment of the current situation.

"I don't know if negotiated peace is achievable in Ukraine," he said Saturday. "That's what we're trying to find out, but I don't think anyone here is claiming that we're on the verge of a negotiated settlement."

Lavrov said Moscow would not allow a situation in which Ukraine poses a "military threat to legitimate security interests of the Russian Federation."

Lavrov has traveled only infrequently to NATO member states since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and resulting severe sanctions were imposed on Moscow. It is unclear whether Russian President Vladimir Putin will accept Trump's invitation to attend the summit at Trump's Miami golf club in December.

Also hanging over the G20 meeting was the prospect of new U.S. military intervention in Iran. That has put the region, including G20 member Saudi Arabia, on edge. Rubio met on Friday with his Saudi counterpart, Prince Faisal bin Farhan, as well as Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, whose country has been a key mediator.

The Associated Press has reported that U.S. officials have told several Middle East countries and regional allies to be prepared for potential renewed military strikes against Iran after U.S. elections Tuesday and the possibility that Iran will retaliate.
